parent.name: Italian Game: Giuoco Piano
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bc4 Bc5
parent.overview: Both sides develop the king's bishop to its active diagonal (Bc4 and ...Bc5), eyeing f7/f2. White's choice at move 4 decides the character. Slow lines are 4.c3 followed by d3 or d4 and the modern Giuoco Pianissimo with d3 (Re1, Nbd2-f1-g3, a4, h3): White postpones any central clash and the game is a patient manoeuvring battle. The sharper lines are the classical 4.c3 Nf6 5.d4 (Greco's Attack, Moller Attack), where White sacrifices a pawn for initiative, and the Evans Gambit 4.b4, a pawn for rapid development and an attack on f7. The Three Knights 4.Nc3 and 4.O-O are also main subtree moves. Black mirrors development, challenges the centre with ...d5, and has sufficient defensive resources. It is a respected choice used by Karpov and, as a Ruy Lopez sidestep, by Carlsen.

parent.name: Nimzo-Larsen Attack
parent.overview: 1.b3 prepares Bb2 on the long diagonal, a hypermodern way to control the centre and pressure Black's kingside from the flank. Black's two main replies are 1...e5 (2.Bb2 Nc6 3.e3, the most common) and 1...d5 (2.Bb2 Nf6 3.e3, often a reversed Nimzo-Indian). White's usual set-up is e3, Nf3, Bb2 with flexible pawn play (f4, c4, d3, a kingside fianchetto), choosing a central plan after seeing Black's set-up. Black may take a big d5/e5 centre for White to undermine, contest d5 with ...c5/c4 English-style, or play London-like set-ups. Theory is light, most lines are rated roughly equal, and the play can turn tactical once the long diagonal and central files open. It is used as a surprise weapon by super-GMs, especially in online blitz.

parent.name: Vienna Game
parent.overview: White develops the queen's knight before the king's knight, protecting e4 and adding a second guard of d5, and keeps the f-pawn free. That flexibility is the point: White can later play f4 for a delayed King's Gambit (the Vienna Gambit), develop the bishop with 3.Bc4 for an Italian or Bishop's Opening structure (with the Qg4 raid against ...Bc5 and the Frankenstein-Dracula after ...Nxe4), or fianchetto with 3.g3 for a quieter game. Black usually answers 2...Nf6 (the Falkbeer, about 60 percent in one source) or 2...Nc6, and the standard equaliser is a timely ...d5. Theory leaves the opening objectively equal, with little elite use but a lot of club use; it is a surprise weapon that avoids the heavily prepared Spanish and Italian lines. The root is a family, so its character depends on White's third move.

parent.name: Petrov's Defense
parent.overview: Black answers 2.Nf3 by counter-attacking e4 rather than defending e5. After 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.d4 d5 6.Bd3 both sides have lost an e-pawn and the structure is symmetrical, with the e-file the main open line. Black's aim is to equalise by quick development and piece trades; White tries to turn a small lead in development or slightly freer play into pressure, often castling and using the e-file or a queenside castling and pawn storm. The 3.d4 Steinitz line (3...Nxe4 4.Bd3 d5 5.Nxe5 Nd7) and 3.Nc3 (Four Knights transposition) or 3.d3 sidelines give quieter or more varied structures. The main lines are widely played at the top and are known as drawish, though some lines hold real attacking chances for both sides.

parent.name: King's Gambit
parent.overview: 2.f4 offers a pawn at once to deflect Black's e-pawn, build a big centre with d4, develop quickly and use the half-open f-file against f7 (Bc4, Nf3, castling). The root covers both the Accepted lines (2...exf4: Kieseritzky 3.Nf3 g5 4.h4 g4 5.Ne5, Muzio, Bishop's Gambit 3.Bc4) and Declined lines (Falkbeer 2...d5, Classical 2...Bc5, and 2...d6 which is the most played move in the database). Accepted lines are sharp and tactically dense; Black tries to hold the pawn with ...g5 or return it with ...d5/...d6 to ease development. Declined lines are more solid and are chosen by stronger players who want to avoid the chaos. Play is open and double-edged for White's king as well.

parent.name: French Defense
parent.overview: Black plays ...e6 and ...d5, accepting a pawn chain and a space deficit in return for a sound position, and then hits White's pawn centre at its base with ...c5. The fight is over the dark squares d4 and e5. Black's problem piece is the light-squared bishop on c8, hemmed in by the e6 pawn; Black solves it by exchanging it or rerouting it (...b6 and ...Ba6, or ...Bd7 with ...Bb5/a4). White typically uses extra space for a kingside attack (f4-f5, and in the Advance the g4/h4 ideas) or expands on the queenside with a3-b4. Play is slower and manoeuvring, with a lot of pawn-break play. It has a reputation for solidity but a cramped early game for Black. The Winawer (3.Nc3 Bb4) is the sharpest branch, the Advance is the main fight in a locked centre, and the Tarrasch, Classical and Exchange are quieter. The root is one position after 1...e6 2.d4 d5; the structures differ strongly by branch.

parent.name: Bishop's Opening
parent.overview: White develops the bishop to c4 at once, eyeing f7 and discouraging ...d5, while keeping the f-pawn free for f4 and delaying the knight on g1. Unlike the Italian, White does not commit a knight to f3 on move two, so the opening is highly transpositional: after 2...Nc6 it tends to become an Italian or Vienna, after 2...Nf6 White usually plays 3.d3 (or the sharp Urusov Gambit 3.d4), and after 2...Bc5 play is symmetrical and can reach a Giuoco Piano. Theory judges it equal with best play. At master level it is a surprise weapon used to avoid Petrov preparation, not a main line.

parent.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Symmetrical Variation
parent.overview: This is a crossroads reached by symmetrical knight development: 1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6. Nothing is committed in the centre; the character is decided by White's third move. 3.c4 transposes to Queen's Gambit structures (QGD, Slav, Semi-Slav, QGA) and is by far the most played continuation in the database; 3.g3 gives the Pseudo-Catalan (a Catalan-style fianchetto); 3.e3 with Bd3 and c3 is the Colle; 3.Bf4 or 2.Bf4 is the London; 3.c3 is a flexible quiet set-up. Wikipedia and ChessBase describe the non-c4 lines as closed-centre system play with simple development plans and little theory. Black is generally free to develop logically (...e6, ...c5 or ...c6, ...Bf5/Bg4).

parent.name: Scotch Game
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4
parent.overview: White strikes at the centre on move three and, after 3...exd4 4.Nxd4, trades the d-pawn for Black's e-pawn, opening the position early and releasing the central tension (s2). White gets space and quick development, Black gets easy piece play and the choice between active set-ups: 4...Bc5 (Classical), 4...Nf6 (Schmidt) and, less often, 4...Qh4 (Steinitz). The structure is open from the outset, so the game turns on piece activity rather than pawn manoeuvring. It can be played either positionally or tactically depending on the line (s2, s3). Objectively roughly equal: the Classical and Schmidt lines give Black good chances of equality, while Mieses (5.Nxc6 bxc6 6.e5) and the Steinitz are sharper (s1). Kasparov revived it in the 1990s as a way of avoiding the heavy Ruy Lopez theory, and Carlsen, Kramnik and Aronian have used it since (s1, s2, s3).

parent.name: Englund Gambit
parent.overview: Black answers 1.d4 with 1...e5, offering the e-pawn after 2.dxe5 to avoid closed queen's-pawn positions and set tactical problems. The main line is 2...Nc6 3.Nf3 Qe7 4.Bf4 Qb4+ 5.Bd2 Qxb2 6.Nc3, where Black regains the pawn on b2 but loses the queenside attack; the gambit relies on traps such as 6.Bc3?? Bb4! with mate threats on c1. White can simply keep the pawn and, with accurate development, retains an advantage. Strong players and engines consider it unsound for Black, and top-level players almost never choose it. It scores through quick development and traps against an unprepared opponent.

parent.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Three Knights Variation
parent.moves: 1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 e6 3. Nf3 d5 4. Nc3
parent.overview: After 4.Nc3 (reached from 3.Nf3 or 3.Nc3) both sides have developed two pieces and the centre is still in tension; neither has committed. White keeps a choice of 5.Bg5 (the classical Orthodox set-ups), 5.cxd5 (Exchange structures with a Carlsbad pawn structure), 5.e3 (quieter) or Bf4, and Black's 4th move (...Be7, ...Bb4 Ragozin, ...Nbd7 Cambridge Springs set-up) picks the structure. In the main Orthodox lines White pins or pressures the f6 knight and tries to exploit Black's passive light-squared bishop behind e6; Black aims to complete development, castle, and free the position with ...c5, ...e5 or ...dxc4 plus ...b6/...Bb7. The game is usually slow and manoeuvring with the d4/d5 pawns holding the centre; wins come from small structural or space edges rather than early tactics. At 2500 level draws spike (11.7 percent in the Chessiverse data), and it is regarded as one of Black's most reliable replies to 1.d4.

parent.name: Scandinavian Defense: Modern Variation
parent.overview: Black answers 2.exd5 by developing the knight and delaying the recapture, avoiding the tempo lost when the queen takes on d5. The main line is 3.d4 Nxd5 (the Marshall, as the old name had it), after which 4.Nf3 and 4.c4 Nb6 or ...Bg4 give White a space edge and Black quick development and easy piece play. White can also hold the pawn with 3.c4 (Black strikes back with ...c6 into Panov-type structures, or the Icelandic Gambit 3...e6) or play 3.Bb5+ Bd7. Wikipedia/Emms describe the 2...Nf6 lines as the more tactical branch of the Scandinavian, though sound for Black; White usually keeps a slight initiative through development. Positions are usually open or semi-open with Caro-Kann-like pawn formations (...c6, ...e6) and Black often castles short while White controls more space.
